posts.title: I enriched 103 business records with owner names in one afternoon. Here's the 6-strategy approach.
posts.body:
A client needed real owner names for 103 CDL training schools.

The problem: The data had garbage like 'Abetterchoiceabc' instead of actual names.

Traditional approach: Manually Google each one. Weeks of work.

My approach: A 6-strategy Perplexity API search system.

The 6 Strategies:

1. Direct owner search with website URL
2. LinkedIn search for owner/CEO/founder
3. Secretary of State business registration lookup
4. School director/principal search
5. Google/Yelp reviews for owner mentions
6. News/press articles about the school

How it works:

For each school, the system tries all 6 strategies in sequence. First real name found wins. Strict validation rejects non-person responses.

Results:

- 72 verified owners found (70% hit rate)
- All first names extracted automatically
- Progress saves every 5 schools (resume on failure)
- Names like Carla Luig, Steve Menefee, Roberto Reyna, Don Balch

The code handles:
- Rate limiting between API calls
- Name validation (rejects company names, titles)
- Multiple query variations per strategy
- Graceful fallback when strategies fail

Takeaway: Data enrichment isn't about one magic query. It's about trying multiple approaches systematically until you find the answer. 6 strategies > 1 strategy. Every time.

posts.title: I built a system to chat with YouTube videos like they're a person.
tweets:
I built a system to chat with YouTube videos like they're a person.

'What does Alex Finn think about Claude Code vs Cursor?'

Instant answer from his 37 videos.

Here's exactly how I built it:

The problem:

I follow creators who share valuable insights. But I can't watch 100+ hours of content.

I needed a way to search and query across all their videos.

The solution: A RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) system.

RAG = AI that searches your documents first, then answers based on what it finds.

Applied to YouTube transcripts.

Component 1: Transcript fetching

Used youtube-transcript-api to pull transcripts directly.

No need to download videos. Just grab the text.

Fetched 69 transcripts from 2 channels in one session.

Component 2: Vector database

Used ChromaDB to store transcript chunks.

Each chunk gets embedded (converted to numbers AI can search).

1,997 chunks indexed from 69 videos.

Component 3: Local LLM

Used Ollama with llama3.2 for answers.

Fully local. No API costs. Runs on my laptop.

nomic-embed-text for embeddings.

The workflow:

1. python main.py fetch 'https://youtube.com/@ChannelName' --limit 100
2. python main.py index --force
3. python main.py chat

That's it. Three commands to chat with any channel.

Challenges I hit:

- YouTube 403 errors (IP blocking) - solved by using transcript API directly
- Rate limiting after 30-40 transcripts - added delays
- Breaking API changes - updated library instantiation

Takeaway: You can build AI that 'knows' your favorite creators.

Fully local. Zero API costs. Searchable knowledge base.

Stop watching hours of content. Ask questions instead.

posts.title: How I built a database of 246 verified business executives in 48 hours
posts.body:
I needed acquisition targets for a client.

Goal: Find private career school owners with decision-making authority.

The challenge: Public databases have garbage data. Wrong names. Old contacts. Generic emails.

The solution: Multi-source verification pipeline.

Phase 1: Data Collection

Started with Texas Workforce Commission approved schools list.
- 627 schools to research
- Filtered to 444 non-Title IV private schools
- These are acquisition targets (not federally regulated)

Phase 2: Owner Research

For each school:
1. Search school website for 'About' and 'Team' pages
2. Search LinkedIn for company profiles
3. Check state business registrations
4. Search news articles for founder mentions
5. Cross-reference multiple sources

Phase 3: Verification

Only counted as 'verified' if:
- Real human name (not company name)
- Confirmed decision-making title (Owner, CEO, Founder, President)
- At least 2 sources agree

Results:

- 246 verified executives
- 143 schools covered (32% of target)
- 99.5% completion on verified targets
- Real names: not 'info@school.com' garbage

The multi-state breakdown:

- Texas: Primary focus
- Florida: 653 private schools, 81.5% owner coverage
- Georgia: 232 campaign-ready schools, 65% owner coverage

Takeaway: Good data takes work. Multi-source verification beats single-source every time. If one source says 'John Smith' and another says 'Abetterchoiceabc' - dig deeper.

posts.title: I'm building a trading setup detection system that combines AI with dealer positioning data.
tweets:
I'm building a trading setup detection system that combines AI with dealer positioning data.

It watches options flow. It finds high-probability setups. It alerts me before market open.

Here's the architecture:

The problem with trading:

Too much data. Too many charts. Not enough time.

I was missing setups because I couldn't monitor everything.

The data source: Heatseeker heatmaps.

They show where dealers have positioned (GEX/VEX).

Green nodes = dealers will defend the level.
Purple nodes = high volatility, wicks and overshoots.

The system I'm building:

1. Capture heatmaps at strategic times (open, midday, close)
2. Extract GEX/VEX values with OCR
3. Pull technical data (EMA, VWAP, volume)
4. Score setup probability (1-10)
5. Alert when probability ≥ 7

Good setups (from my research):

1. First-touch King node rejection
2. Range edge fade with asymmetric R:R
3. Growing floor with price bounce
4. Multi-index confluence (SPX + SPY + QQQ)
5. GEX/VEX confluence bounce

Bad setups to avoid:

1. Midpoint trading (worst - 1:1 R:R)
2. Multiple-retested nodes (weak)
3. Unwinding/decreasing nodes
4. No index confluence
5. Trading right after map reshuffle

The capture schedule:

- First 30 min: Every 5 minutes (7 captures)
- 10:30 AM: 1 capture
- Midday: 1 capture
- Last 30 min: Every 5 minutes (7 captures)

~16 screenshots per ticker per day.

Tech stack:

- Puppeteer for browser automation
- Tesseract for OCR
- yfinance for chart data
- Pandas-TA for indicators
- SQLite for storage
- Discord webhooks for alerts

Takeaway: The best edge isn't watching charts all day.

It's building systems that watch for you and alert you to high-probability setups.

Automate the scanning. Focus on the execution.

posts.title: Most business databases are garbage. Here's how I verify data.
posts.body:
The dirty secret of data vendors:

They scrape public sources. They don't verify anything. They sell you 'John Smith' when the actual owner is 'Maria Rodriguez.'

I learned this building acquisition target databases.

The verification process I use:

1. Start with the claimed data
Whatever the source says. Treat it as 'unverified.'

2. Check the company website
About page, Team page, Leadership section.
Does the name appear? What's the title?

3. Cross-reference LinkedIn
Search for company page. Check 'People' tab.
Who has Owner, Founder, CEO in their title?

4. Check state business registration
Secretary of State databases are public.
Who's listed as registered agent or officer?

5. Search news articles
'[Company name] owner' or '[Company name] founder'
Local news often covers small business owners.

6. Check reviews
Google and Yelp reviews sometimes mention owners by name.
'Spoke with owner John about...'

Only mark as 'verified' if:
- At least 2 sources agree
- Name is a real person (not company name)
- Title indicates decision-making authority

Results from applying this:

- 81.5% coverage (vs 7.4% from single source)
- Actually usable for outreach
- Real names that match the business

Takeaway: Never trust single-source data. Verify across multiple sources. The extra work is what makes data valuable.
posts.cta: How do you verify business data before using it?

posts.title: The data enrichment industry is broken. Here's what actually works.
tweets:
The data enrichment industry is broken.

Vendors charge $1000s for data that's 50% garbage.

Here's what actually works for enrichment:

The problem with data vendors:

1. They scrape public sources once
2. They never verify
3. Data goes stale
4. You pay premium prices for garbage

I tested this on 103 CDL training schools.

Starting data had 'owner names' like:
- 'Abetterchoiceabc'
- 'info@school'
- 'Training Academy'

None of these are actual people.

What actually works: Multi-strategy search.

Not one query. Six strategies per record.

Try everything. First real answer wins.

Strategy 1: Direct website search
'Who is the owner of [company] at [website]?'

Often found on About pages.

Strategy 2: LinkedIn search
'[Company name] owner OR CEO OR founder site:linkedin.com'

Professional profiles are gold.

Strategy 3: Secretary of State lookup
'[Company name] business registration [state]'

Officer names are public record.

Strategy 4: Job title variations
'[Company name] director' or '[Company name] principal'

Not everyone uses 'owner' as title.

Strategy 5: Review mining
'[Company name] owner' site:yelp.com OR site:google.com/maps

Reviewers mention owners by name.

Strategy 6: News search
'[Company name] founder' OR '[Company name] opened'

Local news covers small business owners.

Results from 6-strategy approach:

- 72 verified owners found (70%)
- Up from ~10% with single-source
- Real names: Carla, Steve, Roberto, Don
- Not 'Abetterchoiceabc'

Takeaway: If your data vendor gives you garbage, it's not a data problem.

It's a verification problem.

Build multi-strategy enrichment. Or demand it from vendors.

posts.title: How to build a fully local AI system with zero API costs
posts.body:
I built a YouTube RAG system that runs 100% locally.

No OpenAI API. No cloud services. Just my laptop.

Here's the stack:

1. Ollama for local LLM

Ollama runs open-source models locally.

I use llama3.2 for chat.
nomic-embed-text for embeddings.

Install: brew install ollama
Run: ollama pull llama3.2

2. ChromaDB for vector storage

Embeddings need somewhere to live.

ChromaDB is a local vector database.

pip install chromadb

3. LangChain for the RAG pipeline

LangChain connects:
- Document loading
- Text splitting
- Embedding
- Retrieval
- Generation

All with local components.

4. youtube-transcript-api for data

Fetches transcripts directly from YouTube.

No video download needed.
No audio processing.
Just text.

The result:

- 69 transcripts indexed
- 1,997 searchable chunks
- Instant question answering
- $0 monthly cost

Performance:

- Slower than API (30 seconds vs 3 seconds)
- But unlimited usage
- No rate limits
- No usage tracking

When to use local vs API:

- Prototyping: Local (free experimentation)
- High volume: Local (no per-query cost)
- Speed critical: API (faster responses)
- Privacy sensitive: Local (data stays on device)

Takeaway: You don't need to pay for AI APIs. Local options exist. They're slower but free. For many use cases, that's the right tradeoff.

posts.title: The legislative scraper that achieved 99% accuracy (and how I built it)
posts.body:
I needed Idaho legislature data.

The challenge: Government websites are notoriously hard to scrape. Inconsistent HTML. Missing data. Session-based content.

The result: 99% accuracy on 104 legislators.

Here's how I built it:

Phase 1: Website Analysis

Studied the URL patterns:
- Individual pages: /legislators/membership/[ID]
- Committee pages: /sessioninfo/2025/standingcommittees/[CODE]
- Bill pages: /sessioninfo/2025/legislation/

Identified data fields:
- Name, party, district, chamber
- Contact info (email, phone)
- Committee assignments
- Sponsored legislation

Phase 2: Core Scraper

Built basic extraction:
- Fetch legislator list page
- For each legislator, fetch detail page
- Parse HTML for structured data
- Handle missing fields gracefully

Result: 104/105 legislators captured (99%)

Phase 3: Enrichment

Added committee and bill data:
- Fetch each committee page
- Extract member lists with roles
- Cross-reference with legislator IDs
- Fetch bill sponsorship data

Phase 4: Validation

Verified data accuracy:
- Spot-checked 20% manually
- Cross-referenced with official sources
- Identified and fixed edge cases

Phase 5: Dashboard

Built interactive visualization:
- Filter by chamber, party
- View committee assignments
- Track bill sponsorships
- Export to CSV/JSON

Key learnings:

1. Start simple (names and contacts first)
2. Add enrichment incrementally
3. Validate with spot checks
4. Build visualization for easy verification

Takeaway: Government data scraping is possible. Start with high-accuracy basics, then enrich. 99% accuracy comes from careful validation, not clever code.

posts.title: How I process 2-hour audio files that exceed API limits
posts.body:
The problem: Whisper API has a 25MB file limit.

X Spaces recordings are often 100MB+.

2-hour audio = way over the limit.

The solution: Intelligent chunking.

Step 1: Detect file size

If file > 25MB, trigger chunking process.

Step 2: Split with ffmpeg

ffmpeg can split audio into time-based chunks.

I use 10-minute chunks:
- Small enough for API limits
- Large enough for context
- Clean split points

Step 3: Process each chunk

Send each chunk to Whisper API.
Receive transcript with timestamps.

Step 4: Combine transcripts

Merge all chunk transcripts.
Adjust timestamps for correct sequencing.
Output single unified transcript.

Step 5: Handle edge cases

- Corrupted audio: ffmpeg handles better than Python libraries
- Missing frames: Skip and continue
- Rate limits: Add delays between chunks

The code structure:

1. Check file size
2. If > 25MB: split into 10-min chunks
3. For each chunk: transcribe
4. Combine results
5. Output timestamped transcript

Alternative: Local Whisper

Local Whisper has no file size limit.

But it's slower (30+ minutes for 2-hour file).

Tradeoff: Speed vs cost.

Takeaway: API limits aren't blockers. They're engineering challenges. Chunking + combining solves most size limit problems.

posts.title: The complete architecture of my YouTube RAG system.
tweets:
The complete architecture of my YouTube RAG system.

Chat with any YouTube channel like it's a person.

Here's every component:

Layer 1: Data Collection

Fetching transcripts from YouTube.

python main.py fetch 'https://youtube.com/@Channel' --limit 100

Uses youtube-transcript-api.
No video download needed.
Just text extraction.

Layer 2: Text Processing

Transcripts are too long for direct processing.

Split into chunks:
- 500-1000 characters each
- Overlap for context
- Preserve sentence boundaries

Layer 3: Embedding

Convert text chunks to vectors.

Using nomic-embed-text via Ollama.

Each chunk becomes a 768-dimensional vector.
Similar content = similar vectors.

Layer 4: Vector Storage

ChromaDB stores embeddings.

Local database file.
No external service.
Fast retrieval.

Layer 5: Retrieval

When you ask a question:

1. Convert question to vector
2. Find most similar chunks
3. Return top 5 matches

Layer 6: Generation

Take retrieved chunks + your question.

Send to LLM (llama3.2 via Ollama).

LLM answers based on retrieved context.

The commands:

# Fetch transcripts
python main.py fetch '[URL]' --limit 100

# Build index
python main.py index --force

# Chat
python main.py chat

# Single question
python main.py ask 'What about X?'

Current stats:

- 69 transcripts indexed
- 1,997 chunks searchable
- 2 channels (marketing + AI coding)
- 100% local processing
- $0 monthly cost

Takeaway: RAG isn't magic.

It's: Collect → Chunk → Embed → Store → Retrieve → Generate.

Each step is simple. The combination is powerful.

Capture lat/lng coordinates.

Store all marked positions.
Display count in sidebar.

Removes all markers.

- Road geometry data
- Polyline rendering
- Complex coordinate matching

But for real estate marketing? Position markers work fine.

- Double-click listener on map
- State array for road markers
- Render markers with color based on toggle state
- Clear function to reset array

The UX:

- Visual feedback on click (color indicates action)
- Counter shows number of roads marked
- Clear button for easy reset

Result:

User can 'highlight' roads by double-clicking.
Not perfect. But functional.

posts.title: How I handle YouTube rate limiting (after getting blocked)
posts.body:
The problem:

Fetching YouTube transcripts at scale.

After ~30-40 transcripts, YouTube starts rate limiting.

The symptoms:
- 403 errors
- Timeout failures
- Partial data

The solutions I implemented:

1. Request delays

Add sleep between requests.

time.sleep(2) between each transcript fetch.

Slower but more reliable.

2. Session management

Don't reuse sessions infinitely.

Create new session every 20-30 requests.

3. Fallback methods

If youtube-transcript-api fails, try:
- Different API endpoint
- Browser-based fetch
- Cached results

4. Progress saving

Save state every 10 transcripts.

If rate limited, resume from last checkpoint.

5. Batch limits

Don't try to fetch 500 transcripts at once.

Batch into groups of 30-40.
Wait between batches.

6. Error handling

try:
    fetch_transcript(video_id)
except RateLimitError:
    save_progress()
    wait_and_retry()

The results:

- 69 transcripts fetched successfully
- Across 2 channels
- No permanent blocks
- All data captured

Key learning:

Respect rate limits. They exist for a reason.

Slow and steady beats fast and blocked.

Takeaway: API rate limiting is a feature, not a bug. Design your system to work within limits. Add delays. Save progress. Resume on failure.

posts.title: Third-party APIs often beat official APIs
posts.body:
Twitter API: $100/month minimum.
Apify Twitter scrapers: $0.40 per 1000 tweets.

YouTube API: Complex OAuth, strict quotas.
youtube-transcript-api: Simple, direct transcript access.

The official API isn't always the best option.

When to use third-party:

1. Cost

Official Twitter API pricing is designed for enterprises.
Apify actors work for individuals and small teams.

2. Simplicity

YouTube Data API requires:
- OAuth setup
- Credential management
- Quota tracking

youtube-transcript-api requires:
- pip install
- One function call

3. Features

Sometimes third-party tools do things official APIs don't.

Apify can scrape public data that APIs don't expose.

When to use official:

1. Reliability

Official APIs have SLAs and support.
Third-party can break without notice.

2. TOS compliance

For production apps, official APIs are safer.

3. Real-time data

Official APIs often have webhooks and streaming.
Third-party is usually batch/scraping.

My approach:

- Prototyping: Third-party (fast, cheap)
- Personal tools: Third-party (good enough)
- Production: Evaluate both options

Takeaway: Don't default to official APIs. Compare options. Third-party often wins on cost and simplicity.
